evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.10.1: cupiō tē ad mē venīre
Suet. Jul. 37: vēnī, vīdī, vīcī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday verb for coming. Where to is expressed as with īre (see go): Rōmam, domum, ad nōs, ad cēnam venīre. “Come here!” is Venī hūc! (Traupman 33) or Ades! (see come here).

phrases.latin: vēnit ad nōs Cicerō tuus ad cēnam, cum Pompōnia forīs cēnāret.
phrases.english: your Cicero came to us for dinner, as Pomponia was dining out.

phrases.latin: Ego vērō cupiō tē ad mē venīre, sed viam timeō.
phrases.english: I do want you to come to me, but I’m afraid of the journey.

phrases.latin: vīn’ ad tē ad cēnam veniam?
phrases.english: shall I come to yours for dinner?

sources: Lewis & Short: venio
